faq.q: Is macrognathia always a sign of a syndrome?

faq.a: Yes, the disproportion leads to malocclusion, crowding and increased risk of periodontal disease.
Stabilise airway and nutrition (e.g., CPAP and nasogastric feeding) while arranging genetic assessment.

exam: What bedside signs would you look for to differentiate macrognathia due to Beckwith‑Wiedemann from isolated mandibular prognathism? — Look for overgrowth (macrocephaly, organomegaly), neonatal hypoglycaemia, and abdominal wall defects.

A 3‑month‑old with a protruding chin presents with snoring. Which investigation is most useful when genetic testing is unavailable? — Detailed facial anthropometry and abdominal ultrasound to screen for organomegaly.

Why is CPAP preferred over immediate tracheostomy in a child with macrognathia‑related sleep apnoea? — CPAP is less invasive, preserves speech, and can be titrated while the underlying syndrome is evaluated.

Explain how you would counsel a family about tumour surveillance in a child with macrognathia and suspected Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome. — Recommend abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until age 8, educate on abdominal mass signs, and discuss the low but present risk of Wilms tumour.
During a ward round you note a large mandible but no other dysmorphic features. Which condition is least likely? — Pierre Robin sequence (characterised by micrognathia, not macrognathia).

What drug class should be avoided in a child with macrognathia and suspected overgrowth syndrome when treating hypertension, and why? — Beta‑blockers are avoided if the child has co‑existing hypoglycaemia because they can mask adrenergic symptoms of low glucose.

How would you manage feeding in an infant with macrognathia and severe malocclusion when specialised bottles are not available? — Use a nasogastric tube for short‑term nutrition while arranging orthodontic referral.

A patient with macrognathia develops sudden chest pain and dyspnoea. What red‑flag complication should you consider and what is the immediate action? — Pulmonary embolism from obstructive sleep apnoea‑related hypoxia; obtain urgent oxygen and arrange CT pulmonary angiography if possible.
ai.title: Macrognathia and Associated Syndromes
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Macrognathia is an enlarged mandible seen in several congenital syndromes. Recognising the pattern helps direct investigations and management, especially where resources are limited.

b: Assess facial proportions; compare lower to upper third of face
Palpate mandible for bony prominence
sections.p: Macrognathia is a clinically evident increase in mandibular size, often measured by a lower facial height > 2 SD above age‑matched norms or a chin‑to‑nose distance markedly exceeding the upper facial height.

b: Mild: cosmetic concern only
Moderate: mild speech or chewing difficulty
Severe: airway obstruction, severe malocclusion
sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of facial disproportion and functional impact (speech, airway, occlusion).

b: Beckwith‑Wiedemann syndrome – overgrowth, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycaemia
Pierre Robin sequence – micrognathia (contrasting), but macrognathia may appear after mandibular distraction
Crouzon syndrome – craniosynostosis with mid‑face hypoplasia and relative mandibular prominence
Sotos syndrome – tall stature, learning difficulties, macrocephaly, and large jaw
sections.p: Macrognathia is most often a phenotypic feature of a genetic syndrome; in low‑resource settings, consider common syndromic causes before isolated skeletal disorders.

b: Visible lower facial third > 50 % of total face height
Mouth opening may be limited by dental malocclusion
Snoring or witnessed apnoeas at night
sections.p: Patients present with a protruding chin, difficulty fitting dental prostheses, speech articulation problems, and in severe cases, obstructive sleep apnoea.
Targeted investigations confirm the underlying syndrome and assess complications.

t.b: Quantifies proportion; helps track progression and compare to normative data
Looks for rib anomalies in Beckwith‑Wiedemann; if unavailable, rely on clinical skeletal survey
Detects organomegaly or nephromegaly in overgrowth syndromes; if not available, use physical exam for hepatomegaly
Confirms Beckwith‑Wiedemann; if unavailable, diagnosis rests on clinical criteria

b: Severe obstructive sleep apnoea → risk of pulmonary hypertension
Feeding intolerance → failure to thrive in infants
Neonatal hypoglycaemia (Beckwith‑Wiedemann) → seizures
sections.p: Complications arise from airway obstruction, feeding difficulties, and associated organ overgrowth.

b: Airway: CPAP or mandibular advancement devices; refer for surgical mandibular distraction if severe
Feeding: nasogastric feeding or specialised bottles in infants
Growth monitoring: regular weight/height charts; treat hypoglycaemia with glucose infusion
Dental: orthodontic referral for occlusal correction
sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: treat the underlying syndrome, protect the airway, and address dental/orthopaedic issues.

b: Every 6 months: growth chart, airway assessment, dental check
Screen for embryonal tumours (Wilms, hepatoblastoma) in Beckwith‑Wiedemann with abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until age 8
sections.p: Regular review by a paediatrician, geneticist and dental team prevents long‑term morbidity.

b: Isolated mandibular prognathism – no systemic features, usually familial
Micrognathia – seen in Pierre Robin sequence, opposite facial proportion
sections.p: Macrognathia may be mistaken for isolated mandibular prognathism or for the opposite phenotype, micrognathia.

b: Normal abdominal ultrasound early in life does not rule out later tumour risk in Beckwith‑Wiedemann
Absence of obvious dysmorphic features does not exclude a mild variant of a syndrome
sections.p: Normal imaging does not exclude a genetic syndrome; many overgrowth features are subtle early on.
